title: Why Do Dogs Dig and Circle Their Bed Before Lying Down? (Ancient Instinct)
description:
That frantic scratching and circling before your dog finally flops down isn't random. It's one of the oldest instincts a dog has. In this video we break down exactly where it comes from and why it hasn't disappeared, even on a perfectly soft bed.

script: That frantic scratching and circling your dog does before finally flopping down isn't random, it's one of the oldest instincts a dog carries, inherited directly from wild ancestors who didn't have the luxury of a soft cushioned bed. In the wild, digging and circling served a real, practical purpose, flattening grass or leaves into a more comfortable shape, checking the ground for anything dangerous like insects or sharp debris, and even adjusting body temperature by exposing cooler earth underneath in hot weather. Circling specifically also relates to an old safety habit, turning in a circle let an animal get one last look around before settling into a vulnerable, sleeping position, essentially confirming the area was safe before letting their guard down. Your dog's bed at home is already perfectly soft, there's no grass to flatten and no danger to check for, but that ancient wiring doesn't know that, it fires off the exact same sequence anyway. It's a great example of how much old instinct is still running quietly underneath completely modern, comfortable behavior. Next time you watch your dog spin three times before flopping down with a sigh, you're watching a genuinely ancient ritual playing out in your living room.
